entries.question: Armando controls [Mana Reflection] and taps [Pyromancer's Goggles] to add {R}{R}. They spend one mana to cast [Into the Fray]. Later in the phase they spend the other mana to cast [Galvanic Discharge]. Which one(s) are copied?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling that Mana Reflection doubles the mana produced by Pyromancer's Goggles and each produced mana carries the Goggles' copy rider, so spending each {R} copies the respective spell.
entries.answer:
Both spells are copied — one copy of Into the Fray and one copy of Galvanic Discharge.

Why: Pyromancer's Goggles reads "{T}: Add {R}. When that mana is spent to cast a red instant or sorcery spell, copy that spell and you may choose new targets for the copy." That's mana with a "rider" attached — an effect that applies when that specific mana is spent. Mana Reflection says that if you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead. When an effect multiplies mana produced by an ability that creates mana with a restriction or rider, every mana produced carries that same restriction or rider. So tapping Pyromancer's Goggles under Mana Reflection gives you {R}{R}, and each of those two red mana individually carries the Goggles' copy trigger.

Spending the first {R} on Into the Fray triggers the rider tied to that mana, copying Into the Fray. Spending the second {R} later in the same phase on Galvanic Discharge triggers the rider tied to that second mana, copying Galvanic Discharge. The two mana are tracked separately; using one up doesn't consume the other's rider.

Details worth knowing:
- The trigger only fires for a red instant or sorcery spell. Both Into the Fray and Galvanic Discharge are red instants/sorceries, so both qualify; a nonred spell or a creature spell paid with that mana would produce no copy.
- The copy is created directly on the stack — it isn't cast, so it doesn't trigger cast triggers and doesn't cost anything. You may choose new targets for the copy, and each copy resolves before the original spell it copied.
- Any choice made while the spell resolves (for example, an amount of {E} paid during Galvanic Discharge's resolution) is made independently for the copy; choices locked in during casting, such as modes or a value of X, are copied.
- Unspent mana empties at the end of each step and phase, so this only works because you spent the second {R} in the same phase, as stated.
- Player count doesn't change any of this. In a multiplayer game the only difference is that when you choose new targets for a copy, you can point it at permanents controlled by a different opponent, subject to each copy's own targeting restrictions.

One timing assumption: I'm reading your question as both spells being cast during the same phase (so the mana hadn't emptied). If the second {R} were still floating when a step/phase ended before Galvanic Discharge was cast, that mana would have been lost and only Into the Fray would have been copied.
entries.answer_gold: Both are copied. Mana Reflection has a replacement effect that changes the amount of mana produced by Pyromancer's Goggles. A separate delayed trigger is created for each mana.

entries.question: Autumn restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]'s last ability. They put a [Quilled Slagwurm] onto the battlefield as it resolves. Can it attack on their first turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion and core ruling as the reference — the creature is put onto the battlefield as part of the restart before the first turn begins, so it has been controlled continuously and can attack.
entries.answer:
Yes. Quilled Slagwurm can attack on Autumn's first turn of the restarted game.

Why: A creature can't attack unless its controller has controlled it continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn (this is "summoning sickness"; haste bypasses it, and Quilled Slagwurm doesn't have haste). When Karn Liberated's −14 ability resolves, the game is restarted and the non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated are put onto the battlefield under Autumn's control as part of that restart — that happens before the new game's first turn begins, during the game's setup. So by the time Autumn's first turn starts, Autumn has already controlled Quilled Slagwurm since before that turn began, satisfying the continuous-control requirement. The same reasoning lets those permanents use {T} abilities on Autumn's first turn.

Practical notes:
- Quilled Slagwurm still has to be untapped and otherwise able to attack (no attack restrictions on it, defending player has no relevant effect stopping it, etc.).
- Whether Autumn's first turn is the game's first turn depends on who is the starting player in the restarted game; either way, on whatever turn is Autumn's first, Quilled Slagwurm is not summoning sick. Note that a player taking the very first turn of a game can attack on it — there's no rule against attacking on turn one — they just skip their draw (in a two-player game).
- Everything else about the restart is normal: all players get new starting hands and may mulligan, libraries are reshuffled from all cards owned, and only the cards exiled with Karn Liberated (non-Aura permanent cards) start on the battlefield, under Autumn's control.
- Multiplayer: this doesn't change the answer. With more than two players, the restarted game keeps the same seating and turn order, and any player who had already left the game doesn't come back; Autumn's first turn may simply come later in the turn order, but Quilled Slagwurm is still attack-ready when it arrives.

One assumption worth stating: I'm reading the question as Quilled Slagwurm being one of the cards exiled with Karn Liberated and thus put onto the battlefield by the restart itself. If instead Quilled Slagwurm were cast or put onto the battlefield after the new game's first turn had already begun, it would be summoning sick and couldn't attack that turn.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Karn's ability finishes resolving just before the first turn's untap step, so the creature has been controlled continuously since the turn began and can attack.

entries.question: Abram controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Tropical Island], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Tropical Island a creature?
entries.reason: Both answers state that Blood Moon's effect applies first and prevents Life and Limb from turning the Tropical Island into a creature, so it is not a creature.
entries.answer:
No. The Tropical Island is not a creature — with Blood Moon's timestamp earlier than Life and Limb's, Tropical Island is just a nonbasic land that's a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}".

Why:

- Both Blood Moon ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are type-changing continuous effects, so both apply in layer 4, in timestamp order. Blood Moon entered first, so Blood Moon applies first. (The Tropical Island's own timestamp doesn't matter here; what's ordered are the two continuous effects, and both apply to Tropical Island the moment it's on the battlefield.)
- Applying Blood Moon: Tropical Island is a nonbasic land, so its land subtypes become just Mountain. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type removes its old land types and its old intrinsic mana abilities and gives it the corresponding mana ability, so it loses Forest and Island and gains "{T}: Add {R}".
- Applying Life and Limb next: it only affects permanents that are Forests or Saprolings. At this point Tropical Island is neither (it's a Mountain), so Life and Limb does nothing to it. It never becomes a green Saproling creature, and layer 5 (color) and layer 7b (setting power/toughness to 1/1) never touch it either.

On dependency: you might ask whether Life and Limb should be applied out of timestamp order because Blood Moon changes which objects Life and Limb applies to. Each effect can change the set of objects the other applies to (Life and Limb can turn Saproling tokens into nonbasic Forest lands, which Blood Moon would then make Mountains), so the two are mutually dependent and dependency is ignored — you fall back to timestamp order, which again puts Blood Moon first. Same answer.

The reverse order is the likely point of confusion: if Life and Limb had entered before Blood Moon, then in layer 4 Life and Limb would first make Tropical Island (a Forest) a Saproling creature and Forest land, and Blood Moon would then only overwrite its land subtypes with Mountain — it would remain a 1/1 green Saproling creature land that taps for {R}. Card types and creature types aren't removed by Blood Moon; only land subtypes are.

Number of players is irrelevant here; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.
entries.answer_gold: No. Applying Blood Moon's effect first would prevent Life and Limb's effect from applying to Tropical Island and applying Life and Limb's effect first would not affect how Blood Moon's effect is applied or what it does, so Life and Limb's effect is dependent on Blood Moon's effect and waits to apply until afterwards. Since Blood Moon's effect makes Tropical Island no longer a Forest, Life and Limb doesn't apply to it at all.

entries.question: Aaliyah controls a [Squandered Resources] and a [Glacial Floodplain]. Nicolas controls [Blood Moon]. If Aaliyah sacrifices Glacial Floodplain to Squandered Resources, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: Both conclude Blood Moon makes Glacial Floodplain a Mountain (losing its white/blue mana abilities), so Squandered Resources can only add red ({R}) mana.
entries.answer:
**Only red mana ({R}).** With Blood Moon on the battlefield, Glacial Floodplain is a Mountain and nothing else, so the only mana it could produce is {R}, and that's the only type Squandered Resources can add for it.

Why:

- Squandered Resources reads "Sacrifice a land: Add one mana of any type that land could produce." It looks at what the sacrificed land could have produced — here, Glacial Floodplain as it last existed on the battlefield, i.e. under Blood Moon.
- Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Glacial Floodplain is a nonbasic land (it's a snow dual with the Plains and Island types, but it isn't a basic land), so Blood Moon applies to it. When an effect changes a land's subtypes to a basic land type, the land loses its old land types and, importantly, loses the intrinsic mana abilities that came from those types, gaining only "{T}: Add {R}" instead. So Glacial Floodplain's "{T}: Add {W}" and "{T}: Add {U}" are gone.
- Blood Moon doesn't touch supertypes or non-mana printed abilities, so Glacial Floodplain is still a Snow land and still has its "enters tapped" clause and its "{1}, {T}, Sacrifice a snow land: search for a Plains or Island card" ability — but that fetch ability isn't a mana ability and doesn't produce mana, so it adds nothing here.
- Note also that the mana comes from Squandered Resources' ability, not from Glacial Floodplain, so it is not snow mana (Squandered Resources isn't a snow permanent). "Snow" isn't a type of mana anyway; the types of mana are white, blue, black, red, green, and colorless.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Blood Moon is on the battlefield and unaffected at the moment Aaliyah activates Squandered Resources. If Blood Moon had already left the battlefield (or Glacial Floodplain were somehow exempted from it) at that time, Squandered Resources could produce {W} or {U} instead. This answer is the same regardless of how many players are in the game — Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands, including Aaliyah's.
entries.answer_gold: Just {R}. Squandered Resources cares about what colors of mana it could produce on the battlefield.

entries.question: Noah controls [Compost]. Ainsley controls [Dune Beetle] and a token that was created as a copy of [Bogstomper]. Ainsley casts [Soulscour]. How many times does Compost trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate says Compost triggers once, but the correct ruling is zero because Soulscour destroys Compost simultaneously so it’s in the graveyard when triggers are checked and its ability won’t trigger.
entries.answer:
**Compost triggers exactly once — for Dune Beetle.**

Why:

- **Compost** reads "Whenever a black card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, you may draw a card." The key word is *card*. The trigger checks two things: the object is black, and it's an actual card going to an opponent's graveyard.
- **Soulscour** is a white sorcery that destroys all creatures (they can't be regenerated). Assuming Ainsley is Noah's opponent, everything below concerns her permanents.
- **Dune Beetle** is a black creature card. It's destroyed and put into Ainsley's graveyard as a black card → **one Compost trigger** (Noah may draw a card).
- The **token that was created as a copy of Bogstomper** is destroyed too, and it is black (a copy effect copies Bogstomper's color and mana cost, so the token is a black object). But a token is *not* a card, no matter what it copies. When it's put into the graveyard it triggers nothing for Compost; it then ceases to exist as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked. → **no trigger**.
- **Soulscour** itself is put into Ainsley's graveyard as the last step of its resolution, but Soulscour is a white card, not black → **no trigger**.

So: one trigger total, and since Compost says "you may draw a card," Noah chooses on resolution whether to draw.

Timing note: the Dune Beetle trigger goes on the stack after Soulscour finishes resolving (triggers that occurred during resolution are put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority), so Noah draws after Soulscour is done, not mid-resolution.

Multiplayer: nothing changes for this board specifically, but Compost watches *every* opponent's graveyard, not just Ainsley's. If Soulscour also destroyed black creature cards controlled by other opponents of Noah, Compost would trigger once for each such card. Black creature cards Noah himself controls that die do **not** trigger Compost, since they go to his own graveyard.
entries.answer_gold:
0. Soulscour destroys all permanents simultaneously. Compost's trigger checks immediately after the event in question to see if it should trigger. However by that time Compost is in the graveyard, and its ability doesn't function there.

(Compost doesn't fit the "leaves-the-battlefield" trigger exception because it's a "from anywhere" trigger.)

entries.question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
entries.reason: The candidate asserts Albert knows the choice made when Stalking Leonin entered, but the reference ruling says that choice is not visible after it resolves so Albert cannot see who was chosen.
entries.answer:
Yes — Albert knows which player was chosen for Stalking Leonin, and he knew it before Worst Fears ever resolved.

Why: Stalking Leonin's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability ("When Stalking Leonin enters the battlefield, choose an opponent") instructs Brielle to make that choice as the ability resolves. Nothing on Stalking Leonin tells the player to make the choice secretly or to note it privately, so it's an open choice made during resolution — public information that every player, including Albert and Campbell, sees at the time it's made. There's no hidden-information element to reveal later.

Even if the choice somehow had been hidden, Albert would still see it during the turn he controls. Worst Fears says "You control target player during that player's next turn," which means Albert makes all the choices and decisions Brielle would normally make during that turn, and the player controlling another player has access to the information the controlled player has access to (their hand, face-down cards they may look at, any secretly noted choices). Note that Albert does not gain control of Brielle's permanents — Stalking Leonin is still Brielle's creature and Brielle is still "you" for its abilities; Albert only directs Brielle's decisions for that turn.

A practical aside on the controlled turn: Stalking Leonin's second ability triggers when a creature the chosen player controls attacks Brielle or a planeswalker Brielle controls. During Brielle's own turn only Brielle attacks, so that ability won't trigger during the turn Albert is steering, no matter who was chosen.

Multiplayer difference: with three players, the opponent chosen by Stalking Leonin could be Albert or Campbell, and Albert learns which either way. In a two-player game the choice would trivially have to be the only opponent, so there'd be nothing to learn at all.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield and its choice was already made before Albert cast Worst Fears. If Stalking Leonin instead enters (with flash) later, the choice is still made openly at that time and Albert sees it then.
entries.answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Brielle. Albert can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

entries.question: Arabella controls [Sylvok Explorer]. Nolan controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. If Arabella taps the Sylvok Explorer, what type(s) of mana can they produce?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly allows green — the correct ruling is there are no legal mana types because Gaea's Cradle would produce zero mana, so Sylvok Explorer cannot produce any mana.
entries.answer:
Arabella can produce one green mana ({G}) with Sylvok Explorer.

Why: Sylvok Explorer reads "{T}: Add one mana of any type that a land an opponent controls could produce." The relevant word is *type* — meaning color, or colorlessness — not amount. Gaea's Cradle is a land Nolan (an opponent) controls, and its mana ability reads "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control." Because Nolan controls no creatures, activating Gaea's Cradle right now would actually add zero mana, but the *type* of mana Gaea's Cradle could produce is still green. When determining what a permanent "could produce," you look at what type of mana its mana abilities would generate and treat a variable/zero amount as irrelevant to the type. So green is an available choice for Sylvok Explorer.

Important details:
- Sylvok Explorer always adds exactly one mana of the chosen type, regardless of how much Gaea's Cradle itself would have made. It does not scale with creature count, and it does not add zero.
- If Nolan (or any other opponent) controls other lands, each of those adds its own types to the pool of legal choices; Arabella picks one type on resolution of the mana ability. If Gaea's Cradle is genuinely the only land any opponent controls, green is the only option.
- Multiplayer note: "an opponent" means *any* opponent, so with more than two players Arabella may also choose types produced by lands controlled by opponents other than Nolan. With exactly two players, only Nolan's lands matter.
- Practical reminder: Sylvok Explorer is a creature with a {T} ability, so Arabella must have controlled Sylvok Explorer continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn (or it must have haste) to activate it.
entries.answer_gold: None. Gaea's Cradle couldn't produce any mana, so neither can Sylvok Explorer.

entries.question: Anson controls [Zirda, the Dawnwaker], [Sundial, Dawn Tyrant], and [Mobilized District]. How much does Anson have to pay to activate the second ability of Mobilized District?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the cost is {2}{C}, which contradicts the correct ruling that with both reductions applied in the right order Anson can pay {1} or {0}.
entries.answer:
Anson pays {2}{C} (two generic mana plus one mana that is specifically colorless) to activate Mobilized District's second ability.

How that's calculated:

- Mobilized District's second ability costs {4}{C}: "{4}{C}: Mobilized District becomes an X/X Warrior creature with vigilance until end of turn, where X is the number of creatures you control. It's still a land."
- Zirda, the Dawnwaker says abilities you activate that aren't mana abilities cost {2} less to activate. A mana ability is one that could add mana to a player's mana pool, doesn't target, and isn't a loyalty ability. Mobilized District's animation ability adds no mana, so it is not a mana ability and Zirda, the Dawnwaker's reduction applies.
- Cost reductions expressed as a generic amount only reduce the generic portion of the cost. So {4} becomes {2}, and the {C} is untouched. {C} means colorless mana specifically — it is not generic mana and cannot be paid with colored mana, nor can it be reduced away by Zirda, the Dawnwaker.

Result: {2} generic + {C} colorless.

Note that Mobilized District's first ability, "{T}: Add {C}," is a mana ability, so Zirda, the Dawnwaker never affects it.

About "Sundial, Dawn Tyrant": I don't recognize a Magic card by that exact name, so I can't factor it in. The {2}{C} figure assumes it (or a card named Sundial and a card named Dawn Tyrant, if that's two permanents) has no effect on the cost of activated abilities. If that permanent does tax or discount activated abilities, apply it alongside Zirda, the Dawnwaker: Anson (the ability's controller) applies any cost increases first and any cost reductions after, and the total still can never be reduced below the mandatory {C}. If it's simply a creature with no cost-altering text, it only matters for the value of X once the ability resolves.

Player count doesn't change any of this — the cost is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold:
Anson can either pay {1} or {0}.

There are two effects that are reducing the cost of the second ability of Mobilized District. Because of this, Anson can choose the order in which they will apply. If Anson applies the reduction of effect from Mobilized District first then from Zirda, the Dawnwaker, Anson will pay {1} because Zirda, the Dawnwaker can't reduce a cost to less than one mana. Alternatively, Anson can apply the reduction from Zirda, the Dawnwaker first then from Mobilized District. This would require Anson to spend {0} because the effect from Zirda, the Dawnwaker reduces the cost to {2} then the reduction for Mobilized District reduces it to {0}.

entries.question: Nico controls [Drought]. How many Swamps would Ava have to sacrifice in order to cast [Beckon Apparition]?
entries.reason: Both conclude the {W/B} hybrid symbol counts as a black mana symbol, so Drought causes Ava to sacrifice one Swamp.
entries.answer:
**One Swamp.** Beckon Apparition's mana cost is a single hybrid symbol, {W/B}, and a {W/B} symbol is both a white mana symbol and a black mana symbol. Drought's triggered ability therefore sees one {B} in Beckon Apparition's mana cost, so Ava sacrifices one Swamp.

Details and caveats:

- Drought reads "Whenever a player casts a spell, that player sacrifices a Swamp for each {B} in that spell's mana cost." This is a triggered ability, not a cost or a restriction on casting. Ava casts Beckon Apparition normally; Drought's ability then triggers and goes on the stack above Beckon Apparition, so the sacrifice happens before Beckon Apparition resolves. Ava can't be stopped from casting Beckon Apparition even if she controls no Swamps — she just sacrifices as many as she can (zero).
- It doesn't matter how Ava actually pays for Beckon Apparition. Even if she pays the {W/B} with white mana (or with a Plains' mana), Drought counts symbols printed in the mana cost, not mana spent. Paying with white mana does not avoid the sacrifice.
- Beckon Apparition's mana cost is exactly {W/B} — there is no generic component and no second symbol — so the count is one, never two, and the hybrid symbol is not counted once for white and once for black by Drought (Drought only asks about {B}).
- Drought affects every player who casts a spell, including Nico, its controller.
- Multiplayer makes no difference here: Drought triggers on each spell cast by any player, and the spell's controller (Ava) is the one who sacrifices. The count is still one Swamp regardless of the number of players.

One point of genuine tension worth flagging: Drought is an old card (Mirage) written before hybrid mana existed. The modern treatment of hybrid symbols — a {W/B} symbol *is* a black mana symbol, the same principle that makes hybrid symbols count toward devotion to black — is what produces the answer of one Swamp.
entries.answer_gold: 1. Hybrid mana symbols are the colors of their constituent mana symbols.

entries.question: Bailey controls [Pandemonium]. Anderson casts [Gray Ogre] and targets Bailey's [Jibbirik Omnivore] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Chelsea casts [Incinerate] targeting Anderson causing them to lose the game. Will Bailey's creature die?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes no one can make the "may" choice and no damage occurs when Anderson leaves, while the reference states Bailey (the trigger's controller) will choose another player to make that choice, so the rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
**No — Jibbirik Omnivore takes no damage and survives.**

Why:

1. **Anderson loses the game as a state-based action.** After Incinerate resolves and Anderson is at 0 or less life, the next time state-based actions are checked Anderson loses and leaves the game (704.5a). Since this is a multiplayer game (Anderson, Bailey, and Chelsea), the game continues for Bailey and Chelsea. In a two-player game the game would simply end and nothing else would matter.

2. **Everything Anderson owned leaves the game.** Gray Ogre leaves the game along with Anderson, and any objects on the stack Anderson controlled cease to exist (800.4a).

3. **The Pandemonium trigger itself does not cease to exist.** Bailey controls Pandemonium, so Bailey is the controller of the triggered ability (603.3a) — even though Pandemonium's own wording lets *that creature's controller* (Anderson) pick the target, which is why Anderson chose Jibbirik Omnivore. A card's specific text overrides the default "controller of the ability chooses targets" rule. Because Bailey controls the ability, it stays on the stack after Anderson is gone.

4. **But the ability can't do anything.** Pandemonium reads that *that creature's controller may have it deal damage equal to its power*. The player who must make that "may" choice — Anderson — is no longer in the game, so the choice is never made and no damage is dealt (608.2b: instructions that can't be carried out are ignored). The trigger resolves and does nothing, then goes to the graveyard/ceases to exist. Jibbirik Omnivore is untouched regardless of its printed toughness.

Contrast worth knowing: if Chelsea had instead killed Gray Ogre (or exiled it) while the trigger was on the stack but Anderson stayed in the game, the trigger would still resolve and Anderson could still have Gray Ogre deal damage equal to its last-known power to Jibbirik Omnivore, since a source that has left the battlefield can still deal damage using last known information. It's specifically Anderson *leaving the game* — taking away the decision-maker — that blanks the trigger here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Incinerate was cast while the Pandemonium trigger was still on the stack (as stated), so Anderson leaves before the trigger resolves. If instead the trigger had already resolved and dealt 2 damage to Jibbirik Omnivore before Incinerate was cast, that damage stays marked and Jibbirik Omnivore would die to state-based actions if its toughness were 2 or less — Anderson's later departure wouldn't undo damage already dealt.
entries.answer_gold: The triggered ability of Pandemonium includes a choice to be made upon resolution. However the player that is supposed to make that choice is no longer in the game, therefore the controller of the trigger chooses another player to make that choice. In this case Bailey will choose another player to decide whether Pandemonium's trigger will deal damage to Jibbirik Omnivore. Bailey is the controller of the trigger since they control the enchantment that generated the trigger, even though Anderson is the player making choices about the trigger.

entries.question: Alfredo controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Knight Errant]s with magnet counters on them. Nico controls one [Soaring Drake] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nico's legal blocks?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Nico must block one of the Knight Errants with Soaring Drake (cannot decline and cannot block both), matching the reference.
entries.answer:
**Nico's only legal blocks are: Soaring Drake blocks one of the two Knight Errants — Nico picks which one. Declining to block is not legal, and Soaring Drake can't block both Knight Errants.**

Why:

- Magnetic Web gives creatures with magnet counters both an attack requirement and a block requirement, and it ties magnet-counter creatures to each other in combat (a magnet-counter creature is the thing a magnet-counter blocker is supposed to meet). Here every creature involved — both of Alfredo's Knight Errants and Nico's Soaring Drake — has a magnet counter, so no "can't block"/"can't be blocked" restriction from Magnetic Web is being violated no matter which Knight Errant is blocked.
- "Blocks if able" is a *requirement*, not an option. When declaring blockers, the defending player must choose a legal block that obeys the maximum possible number of requirements without violating any restriction. Since Soaring Drake is untapped and there is at least one attacking creature it can legally block, "no blocks" obeys zero requirements while "block a Knight Errant" obeys one — so the no-block declaration is illegal.
- A creature can block only one attacking creature unless an effect says otherwise. Soaring Drake has no such ability, so it can't satisfy the requirement "twice" by blocking both Knight Errants. One requirement is the maximum obtainable, and either Knight Errant satisfies it equally, so Nico freely chooses.
- Soaring Drake's flying is irrelevant to legality: flying restricts who can block Soaring Drake, not what Soaring Drake can block.

Practical warning (not a legality issue): Knight Errant has flanking. Flanking triggers when Knight Errant becomes blocked by a creature without flanking, giving Soaring Drake -1/-1 until end of turn. So the blocking Soaring Drake becomes 1/1, deals 1 damage to Knight Errant, and dies to Knight Errant's 2 damage. That happens after blockers are declared, so it doesn't excuse Nico from blocking.

If Soaring Drake were tapped, or if some effect said it couldn't block, or if all attackers were unblockable by it, then the requirement simply couldn't be met and no block would be required.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players. Requirements and restrictions are evaluated only for the player who is the defending player in that combat (or each defending player separately, for their own creatures and the attackers attacking them). If Alfredo's Knight Errants were attacking different players, each defending player's magnet-counter creatures would independently have to block one of the magnet-counter attackers attacking that player, if able.
entries.answer_gold: Nico can block either Knight Errant with their Magnetic Web. When declaring blockers, Nico must fulfill the maximum number of requirements, while not violating any restrictions.

entries.question: Avery controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Turn to Frog leaves Wayward Angel a 1/1 green Frog with no threshold effects, while the reference concludes the threshold changes persist so it is a 4/4 blue Frog — opposite final outcomes.
entries.answer:
**Direct answer:** After Turn to Frog resolves, Wayward Angel is a 1/1 green Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities at all — no flying, no threshold ability, and none of the bonuses threshold was granting it (it is not black, not an Angel, and gets no power/toughness boost), even though Avery still has 7 cards in their graveyard.

**Why the threshold bonuses go away too**

Turn to Frog says the target creature loses all abilities and becomes a 1/1 green Frog until end of turn. Wayward Angel's threshold ability (a static ability that, while its controller has seven or more cards in their graveyard, makes Wayward Angel bigger, makes it black, and grants it an activated destroy ability) is itself one of Wayward Angel's abilities. Once Turn to Frog strips Wayward Angel of all abilities in layer 6, that threshold ability no longer exists on the permanent, so it can't generate any continuous effect — the color change, the P/T boost, and the granted ability all stop applying immediately. This is true regardless of timestamps: an effect from a static ability only applies while the object actually has that ability.

**Characteristics of Wayward Angel after Turn to Frog resolves**

- Name: Wayward Angel
- Mana cost: unchanged ({4}{W}{W}; Turn to Frog never alters mana cost), so its mana value is still 6
- Color: green only (layer 5 — Turn to Frog sets the color, so Wayward Angel is no longer white, and threshold's "is black" isn't applying)
- Card type: Creature; subtype: Frog only (layer 4 — the new creature type replaces Angel)
- Abilities: none (layer 6)
- Power/toughness: 1/1 (layer 7b, a setting effect; nothing is left to modify it in layer 7c)
- Other: still controlled by Avery, still owned by whoever owns the card, and it keeps any counters, damage marked on it, and its tapped/untapped and attacking/blocking status

**Two follow-on points**

1. Anything that gives Wayward Angel an ability *after* Turn to Frog resolves will work normally — Turn to Frog only removes abilities with an earlier timestamp than itself; it doesn't prevent later ability grants.
2. Turn to Frog wears off during the cleanup step of that turn. At that point Wayward Angel is again a white Angel with flying at its printed power and toughness, and if Avery still has seven or more cards in their graveyard the threshold bonuses (black, larger, and the granted ability) resume applying right away.

None of this changes with the number of players — Turn to Frog has a single creature target and no "each opponent" component, so a two-player and a multiplayer game resolve identically.
entries.answer_gold: It's a 4/4 blue Frog with no abilities. Wayward Angel's last ability begins to apply in layer 5. It's removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply, it will continue doing so in later layers. Wayward Angel has the earlier timestamp, so it gives itself trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" before Turn to Frog removes its abilities in layer 6.

entries.question: Autumn, Bethany, and Chaim started playing a multiplayer game. Chaim lost the game, and then Autumn restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Autumn draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Autumn draws because it treats the restarted game as three‑player (Chaim returns), while the reference says it's a two‑player game and Autumn skips her first draw, so they reach opposite rulings.
entries.answer:
**Yes — Autumn draws a card on the first turn of the restarted game.**

Why: when Karn Liberated's −14 ability restarts the game, every player who has left the game since it began comes back for the restarted game, including a player who already lost. So Chaim rejoins, and the restarted game is a three‑player game, not a two‑player game.

The "skip your first draw step" rule only applies in a two‑player game (and to the first team in a game using the shared team turns option, e.g. Two‑Headed Giant). In an ordinary multiplayer game with three or more players, the player who takes the first turn does *not* skip their draw step. Since Chaim is back, there are three players, so whoever takes the first turn — Autumn, as the player who controlled the ability that restarted the game — has a normal draw step and draws a card.

Contrast: if Chaim had *not* returned and the restarted game were a two‑player game between Autumn and Bethany, Autumn (going first) would skip the draw step of the first turn and would not draw.

Other details of the restart worth knowing:
- The old game ends immediately and a brand‑new game begins: life totals reset, everything in every zone (battlefield, graveyards, hand, exile, command zone) goes back into its owner's deck and is shuffled, and everyone draws a new opening hand and may take mulligans normally.
- The one exception is Karn Liberated's own text: non‑Aura permanent cards that were exiled with Karn Liberated stay in exile through the restart and are then put onto the battlefield under Autumn's control. Karn Liberated itself is not exiled with those cards, so Karn Liberated is shuffled into Autumn's deck like everything else.
- Abilities that would trigger on a player losing the game or the game ending don't do anything, because the game has already ended.

Assumption: I'm reading the question as a normal free‑for‑all multiplayer game (no shared team turns) and that Autumn takes the first turn of the restarted game. If you were playing Two‑Headed Giant or another shared‑team‑turns variant and Autumn's team went first, that team would skip the first draw step and Autumn would not draw.
entries.answer_gold: No. The game began with 2 players, so it is a two-player game.. Autumn will skip their draw step.

entries.question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly counts the {2} from Suppression Field as part of the noted mana and concludes {C}{C}{C} is added, whereas the correct ruling is it adds only {C} because the suppression tax isn’t noted.
entries.answer:
Allyson adds three colorless mana: {C}{C}{C}.

Why:

1) Ice Cauldron's first ability ({X}, {T}: exile a nonland card from hand, put a charge counter on Ice Cauldron, and note the type and amount of mana spent to pay that activation cost) is not a mana ability — it doesn't add mana — so Nico's Suppression Field applies and it costs {2} more to activate. With X=1, the total cost was {X=1} plus the {2} from Suppression Field, i.e. {3} generic, which Allyson paid with three colorless mana ({C}{C}{C}).

2) Ice Cauldron notes the mana actually spent to pay the whole activation cost, including the {2} added by Suppression Field — additional cost increases are part of the total cost of the ability, not something separate. So the noted mana is three colorless mana, not one.

3) Ice Cauldron's second ability ({T}, remove a charge counter: add mana equal to the noted mana, spend it only to cast the exiled card) is a mana ability: it adds mana, has no target, and isn't a loyalty ability. Suppression Field explicitly exempts mana abilities, so nothing is taxed there and no extra {2} is required.

So the second activation produces {C}{C}{C}. Because that mana is colorless (not generic), it can pay generic costs in the exiled card's cost and any {C} symbols, but it cannot pay colored mana symbols. It can also only be spent to cast the card last exiled with Ice Cauldron.

Assumption on timing: Suppression Field was on the battlefield when Allyson activated the first ability (that's what the {C}{C}{C} payment for X=1 implies). If Suppression Field had entered after that activation, the noted mana would only have been the {C} paid for X=1, and the second ability would add just {C}; either way the second ability is untaxed because it's a mana ability. Also note Ice Cauldron must be untapped to use the second ability, which is why waiting until Allyson's next turn works.

The player count doesn't matter here — Suppression Field affects activated abilities of all players' permanents the same way in two-player and multiplayer games.
entries.answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.

entries.question: Bobbie has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Angel of Sanctions] that exiled Conrad's [Rotted Hystrix]. Alana casts [Lava Axe], targeting Bobbie. What happens as Bobbie loses the game?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the phased-out Angel leaves the game and Rotted Hystrix returns, but the reference states phased-out permanents are treated as nonexistent so the leave-the-battlefield event isn't seen and Rotted Hystrix does not return.
entries.answer:
**Direct answer:** After Lava Axe resolves, state‑based actions see Bobbie at ‑4 life and Bobbie loses the game. As Bobbie leaves the game, every object Bobbie owns leaves the game with them — including the phased‑out Angel of Sanctions. Angel of Sanctions leaving the game means it leaves the battlefield, which ends the duration of its exile effect, so Conrad's Rotted Hystrix returns to the battlefield under Conrad's control (its owner), untapped, as a brand‑new object with summoning sickness.

**Step by step**

1. **Lava Axe resolves** and deals 5 damage to Bobbie, taking Bobbie from 1 to ‑4 life. Lava Axe is then put into Alana's graveyard. No player gets priority in the middle of that.
2. **State‑based actions are checked** the next time a player would receive priority: a player with 0 or less life loses the game. Bobbie loses (CR 704.5a).
3. **Bobbie leaves the game.** All objects Bobbie owns — hand, library, graveyard, exile, and permanents on the battlefield, including phased‑out ones — leave the game. Any objects Bobbie controlled but didn't own would instead be exiled. This is not a state‑based action; it happens immediately (CR 800.4a).
4. **Phasing didn't protect the exile.** "Phased out" means the permanent is still on the battlefield but is treated as though it doesn't exist — it can't be targeted, doesn't affect the game, and, crucially, phasing out is *not* leaving the battlefield. That's why Rotted Hystrix stayed in exile the whole time Angel of Sanctions was phased out (CR 702.25). But Bobbie leaving the game removes Angel of Sanctions from the battlefield for real.
5. **The exile duration ends.** Angel of Sanctions reads "exile target nonland permanent an opponent controls until Angel of Sanctions leaves the battlefield." That's a one‑shot effect with a duration, not a delayed triggered ability, so it doesn't need Bobbie or Angel of Sanctions to still exist in order to end — when the duration expires, Rotted Hystrix comes back automatically, without using the stack (CR 610.3). It returns phased in and under Conrad's control, since Conrad owns it.

**Player count matters:** I'm assuming a multiplayer game, since three players are named — Alana and Conrad keep playing, and Conrad gets Rotted Hystrix back. If this were somehow a two‑player game (Alana and Bobbie only), Bobbie losing would end the game immediately and nothing that happens afterward would matter in any practical sense.

**On timing:** I've assumed Lava Axe resolved and killed Bobbie with the Angel of Sanctions already phased out and Rotted Hystrix already in exile. If instead Angel of Sanctions had somehow left the battlefield before Bobbie's death, Rotted Hystrix would simply have returned at that earlier moment and Bobbie's loss would change nothing about it.
entries.answer_gold: All objects owned by Bobbie leave the game. However the game treats phased-out permanents as nonexistent, and does not see the leaves-the-battlefield event happen. Rotted Hystrix will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Adelaide casts a [Keldon Champion]. In response, Nico casts [Hallow], targeting the Keldon Champion. When Adelaide attacks with the Keldon Champion that turn, will the damage be prevented?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Hallow can target the Keldon Champion spell and that the prevention effect carries over to the creature, preventing its combat damage this turn and giving life to Hallow’s controller.
entries.answer:
Yes — the combat damage is prevented, and Nico gains that much life.

Why: Hallow says "Prevent all damage that would be dealt this turn by target source." A "source of damage" doesn't have to be a permanent — a spell on the stack, including a permanent spell like the Keldon Champion spell, is a legal choice for a source, and a source doesn't even need to be capable of dealing damage at the time it's chosen. Critically, when a resolved spell (Hallow) sets up a prevention effect targeting a permanent spell as the source, that effect applies to the permanent that spell becomes when it resolves. So Hallow's shield follows the Keldon Champion spell onto the battlefield and applies to the Keldon Champion permanent for the rest of the turn.

Sequence assumed here: Nico casts Hallow while the Keldon Champion spell is still on the stack, so Hallow resolves first, then the Keldon Champion spell resolves and enters the battlefield. That's the only order consistent with "in response."

Consequences for that turn:
- If Keldon Champion was kicked, its enters-the-battlefield triggered ability's 3 damage is also prevented, because the source of that damage is the Keldon Champion permanent. Nico gains 3 life from Hallow (the life goes to Hallow's controller, no matter who or what would have been damaged).
- Keldon Champion has haste, so it can attack the turn it arrives. Its combat damage to any player, planeswalker, battle, or blocking creature is prevented, and Nico gains 1 life per point prevented.
- Hallow is not a one-shot shield of a fixed size; it prevents every instance of damage from Keldon Champion for the entire turn.

Limits: The prevention applies only to damage dealt this turn, and only to that specific object. If Keldon Champion leaves the battlefield and comes back (bounced, flickered, dies and is reanimated), it returns as a new object and is no longer the affected source. If the Keldon Champion spell were countered, Hallow would simply do nothing. Damage dealt to Keldon Champion (say, by a blocker) is not prevented — Hallow only prevents damage dealt by the chosen source.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes. Adelaide may attack a player other than Nico, but Hallow's prevention is tied to the source, not the recipient, so the damage is still prevented and Nico — as Hallow's controller — still gains the life.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Effects that apply to damage from a spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Soul Seizer] (back face [Ghastly Haunting])which has been mutated with [Everquill Phoenix]. Everquill Phoenix is the top component. Naomi controls [Axegrinder Giant]. Ariel then attacks Naomi with the merged permanent. Naomi declared no blockers and the merged permanent deals damage to Naomi. What happens when the transformation trigger resolves if Ariel elects to transform the merged permanent and targets Axegrinder Giant?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly states the merged permanent cannot transform because Everquill Phoenix is topmost, whereas the correct ruling is that the double-faced component (Soul Seizer) can be transformed while merged, producing the back-face abilities even though the merged permanent remains a creature and cannot attach.
entries.answer:
**Nothing happens.** The merged permanent does not transform, so the "if you do, attach it to target creature that player controls" clause never takes effect. Naomi keeps Axegrinder Giant untouched, and Ariel's permanent stays a 4/4 flying creature named Everquill Phoenix (with Soul Seizer's abilities), still attacking.

Why:

- **Mutate/merged permanents:** when Everquill Phoenix mutated onto Soul Seizer as the top component, the two cards became a single permanent. That merged permanent has the copiable characteristics (name, mana cost, types, power/toughness) of the top card, Everquill Phoenix, plus the abilities of every component — so it does have Soul Seizer's "When this creature deals combat damage to a player, you may transform it. If you do, attach it to target creature that player controls."

- **The trigger works, the transform doesn't:** the ability triggered correctly on combat damage to Naomi, and Ariel legally chose Axegrinder Giant as the target when the ability was put on the stack (targets are locked in then; the "may transform" choice is made on resolution). But to transform is to turn a permanent over so its other face is up, and only a permanent represented by a transforming double-faced card can do that. This permanent is represented by two cards, and the card whose face is showing on top — Everquill Phoenix — is a normal single-faced card. Being told to transform something that can't transform simply does nothing; you do not flip the Soul Seizer card buried underneath.

- **The "if you do" gate:** because no transformation occurred, the attachment clause is skipped entirely. Ghastly Haunting never comes into being, so nobody gains control of Axegrinder Giant. Note that even if the transform had somehow happened, an Aura can't just be "attached" while it's part of a merged creature permanent — but you never get that far here.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the sequence as combat damage being dealt first, the trigger going on the stack with Axegrinder Giant chosen as its target, and Ariel choosing "yes" on resolution. If instead Axegrinder Giant had become an illegal target (hexproof, protection, or it left the battlefield) before the trigger resolved, the ability would be countered on resolution for having no legal targets, and even the transform attempt wouldn't occur — same net result for Naomi.

Multiplayer: no difference. "That player" is locked to the player who was dealt the combat damage (Naomi), so with more than two players Ariel could only ever have targeted a creature Naomi controls, and the outcome is identical.

One caveat on a related case, not this one: if Soul Seizer itself had been the top component instead, the interaction is murkier and worth a judge call — but with Everquill Phoenix on top, the permanent unambiguously can't transform.
entries.answer_gold:
The component that consists of Soul Seizer is transformed. The merged permanent is still a creature. It is not attached to anything. The merged permanent has the abilities in the text box of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half.

When Ariel chooses to transform the merged permanent, all double-faced components are transformed. The merged permanent now has the abilities of the back half of Soul Seizer instead of the front half. ([702.140e]) The merged permanent is still a creature as Everquill Phoenix is still the topmost card. When the transformation trigger tries to attach the merged permanent to Axegrinder Giant, it can't attach because the merged permanent is still a creature. It remains on the battlefield because the state-based action that puts auras not attached to anything into the graveyard is looking for the "Aura" subtype, not the "Enchant" keyword.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Gaea's Liege], [Rhonas the Indomitable], and 1 [Forest]. Noel controls 5 Forest. Can Aubrey attack with the Gaea's Liege and Rhonas the Indomitable?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Rhonas cannot be declared as an attacker because attacker restrictions are checked before Gaea's Liege becomes an attacking 5/5.
entries.answer:
**No — Aubrey can attack with Gaea's Liege, but Rhonas the Indomitable can't be declared as an attacker.**

Why: Rhonas the Indomitable says it can't attack or block unless you control *another* creature with power 4 or greater. That restriction is checked while attackers are being declared. At that moment, Gaea's Liege's power is still set by Aubrey's own Forests — Aubrey controls 1 Forest, so Gaea's Liege is a 1/1.

The timing detail that decides this: Gaea's Liege's second ability only applies "as long as Gaea's Liege is attacking," and a creature doesn't actually become an attacking creature until the very end of the declare-attackers turn-based action (CR 508.1i). Restrictions such as Rhonas the Indomitable's are checked earlier in that same action (CR 508.1c), before any chosen creature has become attacking. So when the game checks Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction, Gaea's Liege is a 1/1 (Aubrey's 1 Forest), not a 5/5, and the declaration including Rhonas the Indomitable would be illegal.

What Aubrey can do: declare Gaea's Liege alone as an attacker. Once the declaration is complete, Gaea's Liege is attacking, and its power and toughness become equal to the number of Forests the defending player controls — Noel's 5 Forests make it a 5/5. That does not retroactively let Rhonas the Indomitable attack; Rhonas the Indomitable's restriction is checked only once, as attackers are declared, and a legal declaration can't be revisited.

Secondary notes:
- Rhonas the Indomitable's activated ability ({2}{G}: another target creature gets +2/+0 and gains trample) could in principle raise Gaea's Liege's power to 4+ *before* attackers are declared, but that needs two activations ({4}{G}{G} total) to reach power 5, and Aubrey has only 1 Forest for mana, so it isn't available here.
- Gaea's Liege's own {T} ability (target land becomes a Forest until end of turn, only before attackers are declared) doesn't help either: activating it taps Gaea's Liege, so Gaea's Liege couldn't attack, and it wouldn't raise Gaea's Liege's pre-attack power unless it created additional Forests under Aubrey's control.
- Multiplayer makes no difference to the restriction: it depends only on creatures Aubrey controls. It does matter for the size of Gaea's Liege once attacking, since "defending player" is whichever opponent (or controller of the attacked planeswalker/battle) Gaea's Liege was declared against — attacking a different opponent with a different number of Forests changes its power and toughness accordingly.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as both creatures being declared in the same declare-attackers step. If instead Aubrey somehow got Gaea's Liege to power 4 or greater *before* the declare-attackers step (a fourth Forest, a pump spell, etc.), then Rhonas the Indomitable could legally attack alongside it.
entries.answer_gold: No. All creatures are declared as attackers at the same time. Checking to see if any restrictions affect a potentially-attacking creature is done before the creature becomes an "attacking creature".

entries.question: Alejandra owns a face-down [Progenitus] in exile. Nicolas uses [Ruin Processor] to put Progenitus into Alejandra's graveyard. Where does Progenitus move to?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion—it incorrectly applies Progenitus's replacement ability from exile and shuffles it into the library, whereas the reference correctly states it has no replacement effect in exile and therefore goes to the graveyard.
entries.answer:
Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Alejandra's library. It never reaches her graveyard.

Why:

1. Ruin Processor's enters‑the‑battlefield ability lets Nicolas put a card an opponent owns from exile into that player's graveyard. It doesn't target, and it works on face‑down exiled cards (he just doesn't get to look at it first). In a multiplayer game the only difference is that Nicolas may pick a card owned by any one of his opponents; here he's picked one Alejandra owns.

2. Progenitus has the replacement effect "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." A replacement effect changes an event as it happens, so the move to the graveyard is replaced — the card goes from exile straight to Alejandra's library after being revealed. "From anywhere" explicitly includes exile, and that ability functions in every zone, not just on the battlefield.

3. Being face down in exile doesn't turn Progenitus into a blank object. A card exiled face down is still the card it is with all its characteristics and abilities; face‑down status in exile is an information restriction (players can't examine it) rather than a change to what the card is. So its self‑replacement ability still applies, and carrying it out forces the card to be revealed, at which point everyone learns it was Progenitus.

4. Protection from everything is irrelevant here. Protection only stops damage, enchanting/equipping, blocking, and targeting (DEBT), and Ruin Processor's ability doesn't target and isn't any of those. The card is saved by the graveyard‑replacement clause, not by protection.

5. One knock‑on point: because Progenitus was never actually put into a graveyard, any effect that keys on "if a card was put into a graveyard this way" (the way Wasteland Strangler's ability does) would not be satisfied. Ruin Processor itself has no such rider, so nothing else changes — Ruin Processor is still a 5/8 on the battlefield.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the exiled Progenitus is the card Nicolas chose as Ruin Processor's ability resolves. If Progenitus were somehow turned face up in exile beforehand, the result is identical — reveal and shuffle into Alejandra's library.
entries.answer_gold: The graveyard. Replacement effects must exist before the event in question in order to affect it. Progenitus has no abilities in exile, so there is no replacement effect that would apply to it moving to the graveyard.

entries.question: Amari has [Phyrexian Hulk] and [The Mimeoplasm] in their graveyard. Amari casts [Rise of the Dark Realms] to return both to the battlefield. Can they have The Mimeoplasm enter the battlefield as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk?
entries.reason: The candidate says Phyrexian Hulk can be chosen/exiled to make The Mimeoplasm a copy (provided a second creature is available), but the reference explicitly says you cannot choose a card that is also changing zones at the same time, so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
**Short answer: only if there's a second creature card in some graveyard to exile alongside Phyrexian Hulk.** Phyrexian Hulk being reanimated by the same Rise of the Dark Realms is *not* the problem — it's still in the graveyard at the moment The Mimeoplasm's replacement effect is applied, so it's a legal thing to exile. The problem is that The Mimeoplasm demands *two* creature cards, and The Mimeoplasm itself is no longer in the graveyard (it's the permanent that's entering), so Phyrexian Hulk alone isn't enough.

**Why Phyrexian Hulk is still a legal choice**

The Mimeoplasm reads, in part: "As The Mimeoplasm enters, you may exile two creature cards from graveyards. If you do, it enters as a copy of one of those cards with a number of additional +1/+1 counters on it equal to the power of the other card." This is a replacement effect that modifies how The Mimeoplasm enters the battlefield, and replacement effects are applied to an event *before* that event happens. Rise of the Dark Realms hasn't actually moved anything yet at the instant that choice is made, so every creature card — including Phyrexian Hulk — is still sitting in a graveyard and is a legal exile choice.

(This is the mirror image of the familiar Clone ruling: a Clone entering simultaneously with other creatures can't copy them, because in the pre-event game state they aren't on the battlefield yet. Same principle, opposite result: in the pre-event game state, Phyrexian Hulk *is* in a graveyard.)

If Phyrexian Hulk is exiled this way, it never enters the battlefield. Rise of the Dark Realms can only put a card onto the battlefield from the graveyard it was in; once Phyrexian Hulk changes zones it becomes a new object in exile that Rise of the Dark Realms can no longer affect.

**Why it probably still fails as described**

You must exile exactly two creature cards or none — you can't exile just one. The Mimeoplasm can't exile itself (it's the object entering the battlefield, not a card in the graveyard). So if Phyrexian Hulk and The Mimeoplasm were the only two creature cards in all graveyards, Amari has only one legal card to exile, the ability's "if you do" is never satisfied, and The Mimeoplasm enters as a 0/0 with no counters and is put into the graveyard as a state-based action immediately.

**If there is another creature card anywhere (any player's graveyard):** Amari exiles Phyrexian Hulk plus that other creature card, and The Mimeoplasm enters as a copy of Phyrexian Hulk (a 4/4 artifact creature — Golem, with none of The Mimeoplasm's own text) with +1/+1 counters equal to the other exiled card's power as it last existed in the graveyard. Note that the other exiled card also never enters the battlefield from Rise of the Dark Realms. Alternatively, Amari could copy the other card and use Phyrexian Hulk's power (4) for the counters.

**Two players vs. multiplayer:** the ruling is identical, but since Rise of the Dark Realms pulls from *all* graveyards, more opponents means more candidate creature cards, so the two-card requirement is much easier to meet at a multiplayer table. Also remember every creature card in every graveyard comes back under Amari's control, minus whatever The Mimeoplasm exiles.

**Commander note:** if The Mimeoplasm is Amari's commander, copying Phyrexian Hulk doesn't change that — being a commander isn't a copiable value; it stays with the physical card.
entries.answer_gold: No. The Mimeoplasm has a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield. The game checks for any replacement effects that modify how an object will enter the battlefield before the object has changed zones. So Phyrexian Hulk is still in the graveyard while Amari is making choices for The Mimeoplasm, however they are not allowed to choose an object that is also changing zones at the same time.
